newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian airlines implement 100 percent fare hike.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian airlines implement 100 percent fare hike.

text.p: Airline companies in Nigeria have started to implement a 100 percent increase in local air fares, ticketing officials said on Tuesday.
"Most airlines raised local fares on Monday and this is believed to be based on a directive from the aviation ministry," an officer with a private airline told Reuters.
State-run News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reported on Monday that the government decided to jack up the fares after considering the high operational costs by airline operators.
Aviation ministry officials were not available for comments.
The Nigerian Airline Operators group last month hiked the fares three-fold, but the government vetoed what it called a unilateral decision.

According to NAN, with the new increase including value added tax, a one-way economy ticket to the capital Abuja from Lagos, a distance of about 800 km (500 miles) now costs 6,150 naira ($72.35), twice the old price of 2,990 naira ($35.17).
The airlines have long campaigned for an increase in domestic airfares, saying this would help sustain their operations in an economy mired in recession for years.
In November, the military government cancelled what it called an "insensitive" 100 percent increase in domestic air fares annnounced by operators.
The government announced in this year's fiscal budget in January that airline operators would no longer pay tarrifs on aircraft spare parts.
Airline companies welcomed the concession but said it still would not bring in enough revenues to keep aircraft in good state and maintain high safety standards.
A spate of air accidents in Nigeria since last year, blamed by aviation experts on a tight squeeze in the industry, has given the travelling public much cause for worry.

Industry sources said as many as 60 airline companies were licensed to fly in the vast country over the decade or so of unbridled deregulation of the sector. Many exist only on paper, but most of those operating have fallen on hard times, industry sources say.
